newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Laura Ashley shaken by profit warning.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Laura Ashley shaken by profit warning.

text.p: British fashion and home furnishing group Laura Ashley Holdings Plc on Thursday saw its shares dive after warning that profits this year would be lower than expected.

The retailer, undergoing a radical overhaul under American chief executive Ann Iverson, reported a 57 percent increase in profits last year to 16.2 million pounds ($26.3 million), but admitted that earnings in the current year would not be as strong as expected.

The firm said the need to mark-down prices on its current clothing range would affect first-half trading. "As a result the outcome for the full year, although ahead of last year, will be below current market expectations," it said in a statement.
This hit the shares, which slumped 31.5 pence to 113.5 pence each.
"The company has admitted that it's tough out there," one market maker said, "It's a pretty bearish statement."
But Iverson remained confident about her strategy to revitalise the performance of the group, famous for its flowery print fabrics, evoking traditional English country lifestyle.
Iverson, who made her name in Britain by turning around Storehouse's Mothercare chain, said her recovery programme for Laura Ashley was intact.
She said it would be a three to four year process to reposition the company and to see it begin earning double digit margins.
"I'll be here two years this summer -- I'm really pleased with the progress we've made."
The firm, founded in the 1950s by husband and wife team Bernard and Laura Ashley, lost its way in the 1990s after over-expansion and under-investment.
Iverson blamed over-ambitious sales plans for forcing stock mark-downs.
"We had a very aggressive sales plan in merchandising in the first half and it was too aggressive frankly and the business wasn't ready for it," she said by telephone.

She said the group would mark down stock to ensure it was cleared by the end of the season. But she said the stock problem was due to overbuying and not because of its new style clothes. Last year the firm moved to update its trademark floral print look, following the appointment of Basha Cohen as the new director of design and buying.
"I support very much what is being done and I believe my strategy is correct," Iverson said.
She said the aim was to keep tight control of costs, but exchange rate pressures meant people were "running hard to stand still."
The group said manufacturing had become more competitive during the past year. Iverson said the group would continue to look at ways to reduce costs in manufacturing and monitor it very closely.
Industry sources said they expected retail analyst to cut profit forecasts for the current year from around 22 million and 23 million pounds.

Group sales in the year to January 25 1997 fell to 327.6 million pounds ($532.1 million) from 336.6 million, reflecting the impact of discontinued businesses. The dividend was increased to 1.0 penny a share from 0.5.
Sales last year were up eight percent overall in Britain, but fell nine percent in North America partly due to planned store closures and curtailment of mail order.
Trading in continental Europe was difficult, particularly in France, Germany and Austria. Like-for-like sales on a common currency basis were down three percent in both clothing and home furnishings.
The group spent 13.8 million pounds last year on improved information systems and its shop expansion programme. This year it expects to spend about nine million pounds on expanding its stores.

($ = 0.615 British Pounds)
